strengths: PST addresses a meaningful problem in multimodal NLP: gender stereotypes in images containing interacting social roles. Examining organizational hierarchy alongside occupations gives the evaluation useful breadth.

The occupational evaluation systematically covers 800 ordered prompts and reverses left/right placement. Three human annotators per target and reported Fleiss’ kappa values of 0.88–0.92 support the reliability of perceived-gender labels. The results provide credible evidence of stereotypical associations in DALL-E 3’s paired generations.

The appendices provide descriptor lists, generation templates, annotation instructions, and detailed results, and the paper links code and data. FairCritic’s substantial reduction in aggregate stereotype adherence is promising preliminary evidence.
weaknesses: The principal fairness claims exceed what the metric establishes. Equation 1 averages signed stereotype adherence, allowing opposite imbalances to cancel. Table 1 illustrates this: single-person occupational scores of 50 and −30 become an overall score of 10. Near-zero aggregate scores therefore do not establish parity within occupations or roles. FairCritic needs disaggregated post-mitigation distributions and absolute deviations from parity to support 'near-perfect fairness.'

The mitigation comparison does not establish FairCritic’s claimed superiority. Table 2 evaluates the occupational intervention on the five most biased occupations per gender, whereas Table 1 reports FairCritic over the full set; their initial scores are consequently 92 versus 47.38. Both methods should be compared on identical prompts. A fixed-feedback or text-only ablation is also needed to isolate the contribution of adaptive visual critique.

The single-person baseline uses only three images per identity, making occupation-level amplification estimates highly uncertain. The occupational paired evaluation has one generation per ordered pair, and no confidence intervals or repeated FairCritic results are reported. These omissions particularly weaken the detailed amplification analysis and claims about controlled mitigation versus overshooting, although the large aggregate stereotype shift remains informative.

FairCritic is insufficiently specified in the manuscript for reliable reproduction: full critic instructions, images supplied per judgment, post-mitigation sample counts, and handling of 'Cannot Identify' annotations are missing. The conflicting totals of 944 and 1,952 prompts also need reconciliation with the evaluated subsets. These are material reporting gaps despite the useful resource link.

The evaluation does not systematically verify whether generated people actually occupy the requested roles and positions, or whether mitigation preserves that fidelity. Agreement on perceived gender does not validate occupational or organizational-power assignments. This leaves open whether improved scores partly reflect changed or unsuccessful role depiction. Quantitative conclusions are also limited to one DALL-E 3 setup; broader generalization remains untested.
